Combing of a group

Words: 337 Articles: 4
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
Choose a finite symmetric generating alphabet Σ and one word σ(g) representing each group element, with σ(1) the empty word. The associated paths in the Cayley graph start at the identity and traverse one edge per unit time, remaining at their endpoint after completion. A synchronous combing has a constant K such that paths to adjacent endpoints stay within K at equal times. An asynchronous version permits increasing reparametrizations. The formal language need not be a regular language; regular synchronous representative languages define automatic groups.

Combable group

Words: 213 Articles: 2
Combing of a group OurBigBook.com
A finitely generated group is synchronously combable if it admits a combing of a group with the synchronous fellow-traveller property. Without a regular-language assumption, this is more general than an automatic group. A bounded-rung strip argument gives a finite group presentation, and finite-state row shortening gives a recursive exponential filling bound and a soluble word problem for a group.

Finite presentation from a synchronous combing

Words: 170 Articles: 1
Combable group OurBigBook.com
Attach relators for every identity word of length at most 2K+2, where K is an integer fellow-traveller constant. For any null loop, connect its consecutive combing paths at integer heights by rungs of length at most K. Each resulting quadrilateral has perimeter at most 2K+2 and thus is a relator. The bottom row is collapsed at the identity and the top row is the original loop, so these finitely many relators fill every null word and present the group.
Finite-state row shortening of a combing diagram
Words: 93
Finite presentation from a synchronous combing OurBigBook.com
For a null loop of length n, a horizontal row of its combing diagram is encoded by an ordered n-tuple of rung words of length at most K. If there are D such words, there are at most Dn row types. Between two identical labelled rows one can delete the entire intervening annular band and glue the equal boundary paths. Repeating this leaves at most Dn layers of n bounded-perimeter cells. Thus a synchronous combable group has a recursive exponential isoperimetric bound. This does not require the combing language to be regular or computable.

Synchronous fellow-traveller property

Words: 48
Combing of a group OurBigBook.com
Two paths satisfy the synchronous fellow-traveller property with constant K if d(p(t),q(t))≤K for all equal times, with completed paths held at their endpoints. Checking integer times suffices up to increasing K by at most two for unit-speed edge paths. A synchronous combing of a group requires a uniform constant for all adjacent endpoints.

Automatic group

Words: 306 Articles: 5
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
An automatic group admits an automatic structure for a group: a regular language of representatives and synchronous group multiplier automata recognizing right multiplication by each generator and equality of representatives. Representatives need not be unique. This finite-state description yields effective algorithms for the word problem for a group.

Automatic structure for a group ((A,L))

Words: 273 Articles: 4
Automatic group OurBigBook.com
An automatic structure for a group consists of a finite generating alphabet A, a surjective representative regular language L⊆A∗, and finite-state automata accepting the padded convolutions of words (u,v) in L satisfying ux=v for each x∈A∪{ε}. Symmetry of A and uniqueness of representatives are additional conditions, not part of this definition.

Group multiplier automaton (Mx​)

Words: 228 Articles: 3
Automatic structure for a group OurBigBook.com
A group multiplier automaton accepts exactly the padded convolutions of words u⊗v with u,v∈L and ux=v. The case x=ε recognizes equality in the group, rather than equality of literal words over an alphabet.
Bounded-difference automaton (d↦u−1dv)
Words: 96
Group multiplier automaton OurBigBook.com
For a fixed finite generating alphabet and integer K, use the elements of the word-metric ball BK​(1) as states, together with a reject state and padding-status flags. Starting at the identity, a padded letter pair (u,v) changes the state to u−1dv if it stays in the ball. A padding letter acts as the identity. Final state a recognizes endpoint difference a among pairs whose prefixes remain within K. On a regular synchronous combing, intersecting with the two word acceptors gives the full group multiplier automaton. It does not recognize unrestricted endpoint relations for all input words.
Linear-time multiplication in an automatic structure (∣v∣≤∣u∣+N)
Words: 44
Group multiplier automaton OurBigBook.com
Fix the first tape of a group multiplier automaton and use dynamic programming over automaton states and output-padding status, retaining predecessor pointers. The pumping of a group multiplier automaton bounds the search by ∣u∣+N layers, each of fixed size. This constructs a representative of ux in time O(∣u∣+1) without assuming uniqueness of representatives.
Pumping of a group multiplier automaton
Words: 59
Group multiplier automaton OurBigBook.com
In an accepted padded convolution of words, a loop after one tape ends can be deleted or repeated while keeping that entire tape fixed. The altered other tape still represents the same required neighbouring group element. A shortest representative has a suffix no longer than the fixed number of automaton states; an accepted longer suffix gives infinitely many representatives of the same element.

Small cancellation theory

Words: 415 Articles: 5
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
Small cancellation theory controls overlap between relators or attaching paths of polygonal two-cells. Requiring overlaps to be small compared with cell perimeters gives strong disc diagram structure, shortening algorithms and geometric restrictions on subgroups. The metric small cancellation condition C′(1/6) is a central example.

Subcomplex with no missing shells

Words: 66
Small cancellation theory OurBigBook.com
A CW subcomplex has no missing shells if a cell with a shell-length boundary arc contained in the CW subcomplex is itself contained in the CW subcomplex. For C′(1/6) it suffices that every excluded cell have a complementary boundary arc of length at least half its perimeter with no edge in the CW subcomplex: an arc lying in the CW subcomplex then has length at most half and cannot be a shell's exterior arc.

Greendlinger lemma

Words: 170 Articles: 1
Small cancellation theory OurBigBook.com
For the metric small cancellation condition C′(1/6), every nonempty freely reduced null-homotopic combinatorial word contains a segment of a cell boundary longer than half its perimeter. Such a segment can be replaced by the shorter complementary segment. The diagram explanation uses shells with at most three internal pieces: their internal length is less than half the perimeter. Degenerate diagrams require the disc diagram spur alternative.

Greendlinger ladder theorem

Words: 112
Greendlinger lemma OurBigBook.com
A reduced C′(1/6) disc diagram is a single vertex, a single closed cell, a disc diagram ladder, or contains at least three exposed disc diagram spurs and/or disc diagram shells with at most three interior pieces. This is the strong diagram form of the Greendlinger lemma. It follows from the combinatorial curvature inequality after suppressing valence-two vertices: if there are not three positively curved exposed features, all remaining blocks must occur in a chain. In a nontrivial multi-block ladder its two ends are exposed features. Marking two boundary corners and excluding shells/spurs in the side interiors therefore forces the ladder alternative. This is the width-one case of McCammond and Wise, Theorem 9.4; reduced C′(1/6) diagrams satisfy its arc-reduced C(6)–T(3) hypotheses.

Metric small cancellation condition (C′(λ))

Words: 71
Small cancellation theory OurBigBook.com
The condition C′(λ) requires that every piece in small cancellation theory occurring in a cell boundary have length strictly less than λ times that cell's perimeter. Length counts edges. For λ=1/6, an inner path made of at most three pieces has length strictly less than half the perimeter, so the complementary outer path is strictly longer. The attaching paths are combinatorial immersions and the piece convention is part of the chosen presentation or polygonal complex.

Piece in small cancellation theory

Words: 71
Small cancellation theory OurBigBook.com
A piece is a nontrivial combinatorial path that occurs in two essentially distinct positions on oriented cell attaching paths. These may be different cells or distinct admissible occurrences on one attaching path; occurrences identified by the defining attaching-path symmetry are not counted twice. In a symmetrized group presentation, it is a common initial segment of distinct relator words. Internal arcs of a reduced disc diagram are pieces, because otherwise the neighboring cells form a cancellable pair.

Cobounded group action

Words: 48
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
An isometric group action on a metric space is cobounded if some orbit is within a fixed distance R of every point. Equivalently, translates of one bounded ball cover the space. Coboundedness does not require finite stabilizers, a proper space, or a finitely generated group. Every action on a point is cobounded.

CAT(0) space

Words: 140 Articles: 2
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
A CAT(0) space is a geodesic metric space whose geodesic triangles are no thicker than their Euclidean comparison triangles.

Hadamard space

Words: 121 Articles: 1
CAT(0) space OurBigBook.com
A Hadamard space is a complete CAT(0) space. Equivalently, every pair has a midpoint m satisfying the midpoint inequality d(z,m)2≤21​d(z,x)2+21​d(z,y)2−41​d(x,y)2 for every z. This inequality makes the midpoint unique. Iterating midpoints and using completeness constructs the unique geodesic joining the pair. The squared-distance inequality extends to every point of that geodesic by dyadic approximation and implies Euclidean triangle comparison and geodesic convexity of closed balls.

Hadamard squared-distance inequality (d(z,γ(t))2≤(1−t)d(z,x)2+td(z,y)2−t(1−t)d(x,y)2)

Words: 62
Hadamard space OurBigBook.com
For the constant-speed geodesic γ from x to y in a Hadamard space, the displayed inequality follows by repeatedly applying the midpoint inequality and passing from dyadic parameters to all t∈[0,1]. Applying it on two sides of a triangle gives d(xs​,yt​)2≤s2A2+t2B2−st(A2+B2−C2), where A=d(a,x), B=d(a,y) and C=d(x,y). The right side is the squared comparison distance by the Euclidean cosine rule.

Cubical complex

Words: 618 Articles: 23
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
A cube complex is formed by gluing Euclidean cubes along isometric faces so that intersecting cubes meet along common faces.

Link of a vertex in a cube complex

Words: 36
Cubical complex OurBigBook.com
The link of a vertex v records the local directions from v: its vertices are incident edge germs, and a collection spans a simplex exactly when the corresponding edge germs lie in a common cube.

Nonpositively curved cube complex

Words: 34 Articles: 1
Cubical complex OurBigBook.com
A cube complex is nonpositively curved when every vertex link is a flag simplicial complex. Equivalently, its universal cover with the piecewise Euclidean metric is a CAT(0) space.

CAT(0) cube complex

Words: 9
Nonpositively curved cube complex OurBigBook.com
A CAT(0) cube complex is a simply connected nonpositively curved cube complex.

Hyperplane of a cube complex

Words: 52 Articles: 1
Cubical complex OurBigBook.com
Two edges of a cube complex are parallel when they are opposite sides of a square, with transitive closure understood. A hyperplane is assembled from the midcubes dual to one parallelism class of edges.

Carrier of a hyperplane

Words: 18
Hyperplane of a cube complex OurBigBook.com
The carrier N(H) of a hyperplane H is the union of the closed cubes that meet H.

Special cube complex

Words: 144 Articles: 5
Cubical complex OurBigBook.com
A nonpositively curved cube complex is special when every hyperplane is embedded and two-sided, no hyperplane self-osculates, and no two hyperplanes interosculate. Equivalently, it admits a cubical local isometry to a Salvetti complex.

Self-intersecting hyperplane

Words: 16
Special cube complex OurBigBook.com
A hyperplane self-intersects when two adjacent edges of one square are dual to that same hyperplane.

One-sided hyperplane

Words: 19
Special cube complex OurBigBook.com
A hyperplane is one-sided when its carrier is a twisted interval bundle rather than a product with an interval.

Self-osculating hyperplane

Words: 27
Special cube complex OurBigBook.com
A two-sided hyperplane self-osculates when two distinct, consistently oriented edges dual to it have the same initial vertex but do not form the corner of a square.

Interosculating hyperplanes

Words: 23
Special cube complex OurBigBook.com
Two hyperplanes interosculate when they cross in one square and also have dual edges meeting at a vertex without spanning a square elsewhere.

Fundamental group of a special cube complex

Words: 27
Special cube complex OurBigBook.com
The local isometry from a connected special cube complex to a Salvetti complex induces an injection of fundamental groups. Hence its fundamental group is a subgroup of a Right-angled Artin group.

Wallspace

Words: 332 Articles: 11
Cubical complex OurBigBook.com
A wallspace (S,W) is a set S with walls W={W+,W−}, each a partition into two halfspaces, such that only finitely many walls separate any two points of S.
Such wall partitions encode separation data used to construct a dual cube complex.

Wall

Words: 64 Articles: 3
Wallspace OurBigBook.com
A wall is an unordered pair of complementary halfspaces {W+,W−}.
Halfspace
Words: 13
Wall OurBigBook.com
A halfspace is one of the two complementary parts determined by a wall.
Crossing walls
Words: 40 Articles: 1
Wall OurBigBook.com
Two walls cross when all four intersections of one halfspace from each wall are nonempty. A collection of pairwise crossing walls is also called transverse.
Transverse wall collection
Words: 15
Crossing walls OurBigBook.com
A transverse collection of walls is a collection in which every two distinct walls cross.

Wall metric (dW​)

Words: 11
Wallspace OurBigBook.com
The wall metric is
dW​(x,y)=#{W∈W:W separates x and y}.
(1)

Dual cube complex of a wallspace (C(S,W))

Words: 214 Articles: 5
Wallspace OurBigBook.com
The vertices of the dual cube complex are consistent choices of one halfspace of every wall that differ from a principal choice on only finitely many walls. Two vertices are joined when their choices differ on one wall, and higher cubes fill the resulting hypercubes. The result is a CAT(0) cube complex.
Principal vertex of a dual cube complex
Words: 33
Dual cube complex of a wallspace OurBigBook.com
A point x∈S determines a principal vertex by choosing, for every wall, the halfspace containing x. The combinatorial distance between the principal vertices of x and y is dW​(x,y).
Cubulation of a group
Words: 131 Articles: 3
Dual cube complex of a wallspace OurBigBook.com
A cubulation of a group is a metrically proper action by cubical automorphisms on a CAT(0) cube complex. It is cocompact when the action is also a cocompact group action.
Metrically proper group action
Words: 31
Cubulation of a group OurBigBook.com
An isometric group action on a metric space is metrically proper when, for some and hence every point x, the set {g:d(x,gx)≤R} is finite for every finite R.
Wall-metric properness criterion
Words: 33
Cubulation of a group OurBigBook.com
If G acts on (S,W) and x∈S, then its action on the dual cube complex is metrically proper whenever
dW​(x,gx)⟶∞
(2)
as g leaves every finite subset of G.
Transverse-wall cocompactness criterion
Words: 41
Cubulation of a group OurBigBook.com
The action of G on the dual cube complex is cocompact exactly when there are finitely many G-orbits of finite transverse wall collections. Equivalently, there is a uniform bound on their sizes and, for every size, only finitely many orbits.

Right-angled Artin group (AΓ​)

Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
For a graph Γ, the right-angled Artin group is
AΓ​=⟨v∈V(Γ)​[v,w]=1 whenever {v,w}∈E(Γ)⟩.

Salvetti complex (SΓ​)

Words: 97 Articles: 2
Right-angled Artin group OurBigBook.com
The Salvetti complex SΓ​ has one vertex, one oriented loop for each vertex of Γ, and an n-torus cubulated by one n-cube for every n-clique of Γ. It is nonpositively curved and π1​SΓ​≅AΓ​.

Vertex link of a Salvetti complex

Words: 34
Salvetti complex OurBigBook.com
The unique vertex of SΓ​ has two link vertices v+,v− for each v∈V(Γ). Signed vertices v1ϵ1​​,…,vkϵk​​ span a simplex exactly when the distinct underlying vertices v1​,…,vk​ form a clique of Γ.

In any group presentation these deletions preserve the represented element, and in a free group the reduced word is the identity exactly when it is empty.

∣g∣S​≤d(x,gx)+1,d(x,gx)≤(2R+1)∣g∣S​.

HNN extension OurBigBook.com

Every positive power is then reduced with positive stable-letter length, and Britton's lemma makes it nonidentity. In particular, an HNN extension of a torsion-free group is torsion-free.

If C is proper in both factors of G=G1​∗C​G2​, every central element lies in C. Consider determinant-one matrices (uv​vu​) over Gaussian integers with u+v≡1(mod2Z[i]), modulo their common sign. They act on the Poincare disc model by fractional linear maps. Their origin-centered Dirichlet domain is
D={x+iy:x2+y2<1, 2(∣x∣+∣y∣)≤1+x2+y2}.
(27)
For a nonidentity matrix set N=∣v∣2≥1 and uv=m+in. The group orbit point is (m+in)/(N+1) and its bisector inequality is 2(mx+ny)≤N(1+x2+y2). Since m2+n2=N(N+1), integrality gives ∣m∣,∣n∣≤N, so the four inequalities defining D imply all of them. They are necessary because the matrices with u=1±i, v=±i realize the four combinations m,n=±1. The four sides are arcs of the unit-radius circles centered at ±1±i, and the ideal vertices are 1,i,−1,−i.

Nielsen–Schreier theorem

Words: 129 Articles: 3
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
Every subgroup of a free group is itself a free group. The theorem follows by representing the subgroup by a connected covering graph of a rose and choosing a maximal subtree.

Nielsen–Schreier formula

Words: 81 Articles: 1
Nielsen–Schreier theorem OurBigBook.com
If H has finite index d in the free group Fn​, then
rank(H)=1+d(n−1).​
(28)
Indeed, the d-sheeted covering graph of the rose with n petals has d vertices and dn edges, so its fundamental group has rank dn−d+1.

Rank-to-index limit for subgroups of a free group (rank(H)/[Fn​:H]=n−1+1/[Fn​:H])

Words: 45
Nielsen–Schreier formula OurBigBook.com
For finite-index subgroups of a rank-n free group, the Nielsen–Schreier formula gives the displayed quotient. Along any sequence whose finite indices tend to infinity, the quotient tends to n−1. Subtracting one from the rank before dividing gives the constant rank gradient n−1.

Schreier index-rank inequality

Words: 23
Nielsen–Schreier theorem OurBigBook.com
If H has finite index d in a finitely generated group G, then Schreier's lemma gives
d(H)≤1+d(d(G)−1).​
(29)
Equality holds when G is a free group of finite rank.

Finiteness of subgroups of a fixed finite index

Words: 45
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
A finitely generated group has only finitely many subgroups of any prescribed index of a subgroup n. Every such subgroup is a point stabilizer for a transitive action on n points, while a homomorphism from a finitely generated group to the finite symmetric group Sn​ has only finitely many possible images of the generators.

Growth function of a discrete metric space (βX,x0​​)

Words: 515 Articles: 9
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
For a locally finite discrete metric space X with basepoint x0​, its growth function is
βX,x0​​(r)=#{x∈X:d(x,x0​)≤r}.
(30)
Changing the basepoint changes the argument by at most an additive constant. In a vertex-transitive metric space, including every Cayley graph, the growth function is exactly independent of the basepoint.

Growth function of a finitely generated group (βG,S​)

Words: 469 Articles: 8
Growth function of a discrete metric space OurBigBook.com
For a finitely generated group G with finite generating set S, the growth function βG,S​(r) is the number of group elements of word metric distance at most r from the identity. Different finite generating sets change its scale only by multiplicative constants.

Polynomial growth of a group

Words: 405 Articles: 6
Growth function of a finitely generated group OurBigBook.com
A finitely generated group has polynomial growth when, for some constants C,D, its growth function of a finitely generated group satisfies
βG,S​(r)≤C(1+r)D.
(31)
This property is independent of the finite generating set S.
Polynomial growth of properly discontinuous isometry groups (βΓ​(m)≤∣Γp​∣(1+Lm/ρ)n)
Words: 184 Articles: 1
Polynomial growth of a group OurBigBook.com
A finitely generated group of isometries acting properly discontinuously on a complete connected n-dimensional Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature has polynomial growth of a group of degree at most n. Choose ρ>0 so distinct points of an orbit are separated by more than 2ρ. Let L be the largest displacement of the base point by a generator. The radius-m word metric ball maps into the metric ball of radius Lm, with fibers of size the finite stabilizer ∣Γp​∣. Disjoint radius-ρ balls around these orbit points have equal volume and fit inside the ball of radius Lm+ρ. The Bishop-Gromov inequality bounds their number by (1+Lm/ρ)n, giving the displayed estimate.
First Betti-number bound from polynomial fundamental-group growth (b1​(M)≤dimM)
Words: 82
Polynomial growth of properly discontinuous isometry groups OurBigBook.com
For a compact connected Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, its finitely generated fundamental group acts freely and properly discontinuously on the complete universal cover. The preceding polynomial growth of properly discontinuous isometry groups bound applies. The degree-one Hurewicz theorem identifies first integral homology with the abelianization of the fundamental group. If its free rank is b1​(M), this group maps onto Zb1​(M). Choosing lifts of a basis gives at least a constant times mb1​(M) distinct elements in a word ball of radius a constant times m. The upper bound of order mdimM forces the displayed inequality.
Polynomial group growth from orbit packing (∣BS​(m)∣≤C(1+m)n)
Words: 63
Polynomial growth of a group OurBigBook.com
A properly discontinuous group action by isometries of a finitely generated group on a complete n-dimensional Riemannian manifold of nonnegative Ricci curvature yields the displayed group growth bound. Distinct orbit points are uniformly separated, while a word of length m moves a basepoint by at most Dm. Pack disjoint equal-volume small balls about the orbit points into B(p,Dm+ε) and apply the Bishop-Gromov inequality. A finite point stabilizer contributes its order to the bound; freeness is unnecessary.
One-scale virtual nilpotence theorem
Words: 66
Polynomial growth of a group OurBigBook.com
For every d>0 there is N(d) such that, if a group has a finite symmetric generating set S containing the identity and
∣Sn∣≤nd∣S∣
(32)
for some n≥N(d), then there are H⊴C<G with H⊆S⌊n/2⌋, [G:C]=Od​(1), and C/H nilpotent of class Od​(1). A geometric-scale pigeonhole argument finds a large radius of small tripling, and the Breuillard-Green-Tao structure theorem for approximate groups supplies H and C.
Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth
Words: 28
Polynomial growth of a group OurBigBook.com
Every finitely generated group of polynomial growth of a group has a virtually nilpotent group structure. Applying the one-scale virtual nilpotence theorem gives a finite normal subgroup with nilpotent quotient; centralizing that finite subgroup produces a nilpotent subgroup of finite index.
Polynomial growth of a finitely generated two-step nilpotent group
Words: 39
Polynomial growth of a group OurBigBook.com
Every finitely generated two-step nilpotent group has polynomial growth of a group. If s1​,…,sk​ generate it, centrality of the commutators collects every word of length at most n into
s1a1​​⋯skak​​∏i<j​[si​,sj​]bij​,
(33)
where ∣ai​∣≤n and ∣bij​∣=O(n2). There are therefore only polynomially many possible collected words.

The matrices
A=(10​11​),B=(11​01​)
(34)
generate a free monoid in SL2​(Z). Hence the 2n positive words of length n are distinct and SL2​(Z) has exponential growth of a group.

Amenable group

Words: 507 Articles: 13
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
A discrete group G is amenable when it admits a left-invariant finitely additive probability measure on all subsets of G. Equivalently, it admits an invariant mean on the bounded real-valued functions on G.

Reiter condition (∥λ(g)μn​−μn​∥1​→0)

Words: 55
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
For a countable discrete group, the Reiter condition requires a sequence of probability measures in ℓ1(G) asymptotically invariant under every left translation. It is equivalent to the existence of an invariant mean and a Følner sequence. Separation by bounded functions shows that amenability gives approximate invariance simultaneously on each finite set of translations; countability makes the successive finite tests into a sequence.

Invariant mean

Words: 36
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
An invariant mean on a group G is a positive linear functional m:ℓ∞(G)→R with m(1)=1 and m(gf)=m(f) for every g∈G. Applied to indicator functions, it is a left-invariant finitely additive probability measure on all subsets of G.

Equidecomposable subsets under a group action

Words: 36
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
For a group G acting on a set X, subsets A,B⊆X are G-equidecomposable when there are finite partitions A=⨆i​Ai​ and B=⨆i​Bi​ and elements gi​∈G with gi​Ai​=Bi​ for every i.

Paradoxical group action

Words: 41
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
A G-set X is paradoxical when it contains two disjoint subsets each G-equidecomposable with X. An invariant finitely additive probability measure rules out such a decomposition, because it would assign each copy the full measure of X.

Nonamenability of a nonabelian free group

Words: 33
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
The free group F2​=⟨a,b⟩ is not an amenable group. Partitioning reduced words by their first letters gives two translated decompositions of F2​ whose invariance equations add to 2=1, contradicting the existence of an invariant mean.

A subgroup of an amenable group is amenable

Words: 37
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
Every subgroup of an amenable group is amenable. One proof restricts an invariant mean after extending bounded functions from the subgroup to the whole group along a set of coset representatives. Consequently, a group containing a nonamenable subgroup is nonamenable.

Virtually abelian groups are amenable

Words: 19
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
Every abelian group is amenable, and amenability is preserved by finite extensions. Hence every group with an abelian finite-index subgroup is an amenable group.

Følner condition

Words: 172 Articles: 4
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
A finitely generated group G with finite generating set S satisfies the Følner condition when, for every ε>0, there is a nonempty finite subset F⊆G such that
∣F∣∣sF△F∣​<ε(s∈S).
(35)
The condition is independent of the finite generating set.

Følner sequence

Words: 100 Articles: 2
Følner condition OurBigBook.com
A Følner sequence is a sequence of nonempty finite subsets Fn​⊆G such that ∣gFn​△Fn​∣/∣Fn​∣→0 for every g∈G.
Layer-cake extraction of Følner sets
Words: 64
Følner sequence OurBigBook.com
For a finitely supported nonnegative function μ of sum one, let Ft​={x:μ(x)>t}. Then ∫0∞​∣Ft​∣dt=1 and ∫0∞​∣Ft​△gFt​∣dt=∥μ−λ(g)μ∥1​. If the sum of these latter integrals over a finite set of translations is less than ε, some nonempty level set has the sum of its relative boundaries less than ε. This converts the Reiter condition into finite Følner sets without assuming that the group is finitely generated.
Følner sequence for the integers
Words: 15
Følner sequence OurBigBook.com
The intervals Fn​={−n,…,n} form a Følner sequence for the additive group Z, because
∣Fn​∣∣(Fn​+1)△Fn​∣​=2n+12​⟶0.
(36)

Følner condition implies amenability

Words: 33
Følner condition OurBigBook.com
Normalized counting measures on a Følner sequence have a convergent subnet in the compact product [0,1]P(G). The limit is a left-invariant finitely additive probability measure, so every group satisfying the Følner condition is an amenable group.

Amenability of a free product

Words: 49
Amenable group OurBigBook.com
For nontrivial groups A,B, the free product A∗B is amenable exactly in the exceptional case A≅B≅C2​. In that case it is the infinite dihedral group, hence a virtually cyclic group and amenable. In every other case the normal form theorem for a free product and the ping-pong lemma produce a subgroup isomorphic to F2​; the fact that a subgroup of an amenable group is amenable then obstructs amenability.

Length function

Words: 27
Geometric group theory OurBigBook.com
A group length function L:G→[0,∞) satisfies L(1)=0, L(g−1)=L(g) and L(gh)≤L(g)+L(h). Word length for a chosen generating set is an example; Coxeter length uses the simple reflections.
